$comment: Injection grammar: HTML inside FAST's html`` templates and CSS inside css``, written for this extension (not vendored from vscode-lit-html — task P5-01 chose write-our-own to avoid carrying a fork of another grammar). This half only opens the template and hands the body over; everything that has to keep working *inside* the body — ${…} and FAST's :/?/@ binding prefixes — lives in `fast-element-embedded.injection.json`, because the first four selectors' `-string` switches the whole grammar off the moment the template's own `string.template.fast-element.ts` scope is on the stack. The fifth selector buys back the one place that `-string` should not have taken away: a template nested in an interpolation of another one, which `when(…, html`…`)` and `repeat(…, html`…`)` write every day. It cannot be a pattern on the opening rule — by the time the inner `html` is reached the stack is inside whatever anonymous rule source.ts pushed for the enclosing argument list, and a rule listed on an ancestor is never consulted again — so it has to be an injection too. The negations name TypeScript's own string scopes one by one rather than `-string`, so that the enclosing FAST template (a string) and a binding's `string.quoted.html` value both stay open for nesting.
injectionSelector: L:source.ts -comment -string, L:source.tsx -comment -string, L:source.js -comment -string, L:source.jsx -comment -string, L:string.template.fast-element.ts meta.embedded.line.ts -comment -string.quoted.single.ts -string.quoted.double.ts -string.template.ts -string.regexp

fastHtmlTypedTemplate.$comment:
Everything `fastHtmlTemplate`'s single regex cannot open, because a `begin` only ever sees one line: type arguments broken over several lines (`html<
  ToastItem,
  Toaster
>`…``), and a type argument that is itself generic (`html<Row<Cell>>`). The region runs from `html` to the template's closing backtick, and its two children divide it up — the type arguments go to TypeScript's own `#type-arguments` rule, so they keep the colours they have anywhere else, and the backtick that follows opens the body exactly as above. The end is a lookbehind, so it can only match once the body rule has popped, and it never fires early: while the body is on the stack it is the body's own end that is consulted. `fastHtmlTemplate` is listed first, so for a template that fits on one line it wins the tie and this rule never opens. The second alternative of the end is the escape hatch for something that only *looked* like a typed template — `html<x` that turns out to be a comparison — after which the type arguments close on a `>` that no backtick follows; without it the rule would stay open to the end of the file. The `(?=<…)` guard is what keeps that case rare: a comparison is written `html < count`, with the spaces this rule refuses.

fastCssPartialTemplate.$comment: `css.partial` is the other half of FAST's css tag, and the dot is why `fastCssTemplate` cannot open it: a tagged template's tag is an expression, not just a name. The body is the reason it is a rule of its own rather than one more spelling — a partial is a declaration list with no rule around it (`position: absolute;`), which is `#rule-list-innards`, the CSS grammar's *inside* of a block, not `source.css`, whose top level expects a selector or an at-rule and would call a bare property name a tag selector. `#rule-list-innards` already carries `#selector`, so a partial that does write a whole rule keeps its selector; `#at-rules` and `#rule-list` are listed after it to open the block that follows one. Everything else is `fastCssTemplate`'s: the same `string.template.fast-element.ts` and `meta.embedded.block.css`, so `${…}` inside a partial reaches the embedded injection exactly as it does inside a full stylesheet.
fastCssPartialTemplate.name: string.template.fast-element.ts
